[PATH:empirical] Cross-national survey data (e.g., World Values Survey, European Social Survey) measuring perceived legitimacy of inequality (e.g., agreement with 'differences in income are acceptable') and interpersonal trust, analyzed with multilevel models for OECD countries post-1980. — Directly tests the interaction between income inequality and perceived legitimacy on trust, controlling for welfare state strength and other confounds.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental studies (e.g., vignette or lab-in-the-field experiments) manipulating perceived legitimacy of inequality (e.g., via information about meritocracy vs. unfair advantage) and measuring trust behavior in economic games across high-inequality contexts. — Establishes causal direction: whether legitimacy perceptions moderate the inequality-trust link, isolating mechanism from observational confounds.

[PATH:literature] Comparative case studies of OECD countries with similar high inequality but differing cultural narratives about legitimacy (e.g., US vs. Nordic welfare states), using historical and qualitative data on trust trends. — Provides contextual depth and qualitative evidence for how perceived legitimacy shapes the inequality-trust relationship, complementing quantitative findings.

C011.subject: inequality of opportunity (as distinct from inequality of outcomes)
C011.object: social cohesion more strongly than inequality of outcomes, even when controlling for overall wealth inequality
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: inequality of opportunity (as distinct from inequality of outcomes) social cohesion more strongly than inequality of outcomes, even when controlling for overall wealth inequality]

[PATH:empirical] World Values Survey (WVS) and European Social Survey (ESS) data on social trust and perceived fairness, combined with the World Bank's Human Opportunity Index for OECD countries (2000-2020) — Multi-level regression analyses using these datasets can directly test whether inequality of opportunity (measured by the Human Opportunity Index) has a stronger negative association with social cohesion indicators (e.g., generalized trust, civic participation) than income inequality (Gini coefficient), controlling for overall wealth distribution.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel studies like the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) or the British Household Panel Survey (BHPS/UKHLS) — Individual-level panel data allow within-country analysis over time to isolate effects of perceived opportunity inequality (e.g., perceived fairness of social mobility) on social cohesion measures, controlling for actual income/wealth inequality, thus providing stronger causal inference than cross-national correlations.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical frameworks from political philosophy (e.g., John Rawls' 'justice as fairness') and social psychology (e.g., relative deprivation theory, system justification theory) — These theories predict that perceived unfairness in opportunity (rather than outcome gaps per se) triggers resentment and erodes trust. A systematic review of experimental and quasi-experimental studies testing these mechanisms would clarify the causal pathways and boundary conditions of the hypothesis.
